findings.title: New abstract method order() breaks all existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: The PR adds `int order();` as a new abstract method on the public `CryptoProvider` SPI. Only the four implementations in this repository were updated. Any third-party or downstream implementation of this interface (this is the documented SPI for plugging in crypto providers, loaded via ServiceLoader in CryptoIntegration) will fail to compile against the new keycloak-common, and — worse — an existing compiled provider jar on the classpath will throw AbstractMethodError at runtime when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` sorts providers by calling `order()`, breaking previously working deployments at startup. The method should be given a default (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) to preserve backward compatibility, as was already done for other methods on this interface (`getSupportedKeyStoreTypes`, `getSupportedRsaKeySizes`).

findings.title: Multiple same-order providers are now silently accepted instead of failing fast
findings.body: Previously, having more than one CryptoProvider on the classpath caused a hard `IllegalStateException` ("Multiple crypto providers loaded... Make sure only one cryptoProvider available on the classpath"). Now `detectProvider` sorts by `order()` descending and silently uses the first one, merely logging the rest at debug level. DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider and WildFlyElytronProvider are all assigned order 200, so if two of them end up on the classpath together (exactly the misconfiguration the old error guarded against), the winner is decided by ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order. In particular, a FIPS deployment that accidentally also ships the default (non-FIPS) provider jar will silently run non-FIPS-compliant crypto instead of failing at startup. The fail-fast check should be retained for ties at the highest order, or the FIPS provider should be given a strictly higher order.

findings.title: ECDSA test only round-trips through its own encoder/decoder and never validates the DER output
findings.body: The test takes a JDK-produced DER signature, converts it to concatenated R||S, converts back to DER with the new ASN1Encoder, decodes again with the new ASN1Decoder, and asserts the two concatenated forms are equal. Because both conversions share the same new implementation, a systematic encoder bug that the matching decoder tolerates (e.g. swapped r/s integers, wrong integer sign/zero-padding handling) still passes the assertion. The test never checks that the re-encoded DER byte array is actually valid — e.g. by verifying `asn1Des` with `Signature.getInstance(...)` initialized with the public key, or by comparing it against the original JDK-produced `sign` bytes / a known-good implementation such as the existing BouncyCastle-based ECDSACryptoProvider. As written, the test would not catch an encoder that produces signatures no real verifier accepts.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which returns whatever JCA provider supplies the default keystore type (typically the SUN provider) — it has nothing to do with BouncyCastle. Callers of this method (e.g. `BouncyIntegration.init()`, which registers the returned provider and then uses `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` as the provider name for `Cipher`/`KeyFactory`/`Signature.getInstance(alg, PROVIDER)` calls) will be handed the SUN provider under the assumption it is BouncyCastle, causing failures for algorithms/paddings only BC provides (e.g. "AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding") or silently using a different provider than intended. If there is no BouncyCastle on the classpath this method should return null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) rather than a mislabelled unrelated provider.

findings.title: Indefinite-length form returns -1 and later causes unchecked NegativeArraySizeException
findings.body: `readLength()` returns -1 for the BER indefinite-length marker (0x80). Callers pass this straight into `read(int length)`, which does `new byte[length]` — so a signature blob containing a 0x80 length byte throws an unchecked `NegativeArraySizeException` instead of the `IOException` callers expect for malformed input. Since this decoder parses externally supplied signature bytes, malformed input should be rejected with a checked IOException (or the indefinite-length case explicitly disallowed, since DER never uses it).

findings.title: Dead encoder instances created and discarded in concatenatedRSToASN1DER
findings.body: Lines 114-115 call `ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger)` and `ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger)` and discard the results; the actual DER is built again immediately below in the `writeDerSeq(...)` call. The two discarded statements are leftover dead code and should be removed to avoid confusion about which encoding path is authoritative.
